Yes. **Stop there—don't lose the remaining evidence.** You've captured exactly what we needed, and there is already something significant here.

### What we know from this new test

At **22:31–22:33 on 10 Oct**, you started the *next* video in your `FlowStateNerobiology...` playlist:

**“The science of effortlessness: How to…” — Big Think**

And **right at the start**, YouTube served an **ad pod of 2 ads**.

**Ad 1 — Specsavers**

The interesting part is that you captured Google's own **“Why you're seeing this ad”** panel. It explicitly says information used included:

- **Your age**
- **The video you're watching**
- **Time of day or your general location** (country/city)
- **Google's estimation of your interests**, based on your signed-in Google activity

So this gives us much stronger evidence than our earlier speculation. Google itself is telling you this Specsavers impression wasn't necessarily based on one single reason. **Context + account/audience information + location/time + inferred interests were all inputs.**

There's another interesting detail in the creative itself: the tiny disclaimer says it is **funded by the Scottish Government and available in Scotland only**. So geographic relevance looks particularly important for this Specsavers campaign.

**Ad 2 — Baseten Labs**

This one is *much more interesting for our product/distribution investigation*.

The creative says:

> **“There's no textbook. Now there is.”**

and shows an **Inference Engineering** book for engineers working with technologies powering AI companies/applications.

That's remarkably aligned with the kind of **AI/engineering material** you consume, while the actual Big Think video is about **flow/effortlessness**, not AI inference engineering.

But we should **not yet claim that Google targeted Baseten because it knows you're interested in AI**. That's exactly why your **two missing screenshots matter**. We need Baseten's own **“Why you're seeing this ad”** section.

### Send the remaining 2 when ChatGPT allows it

Don't worry about the photo limit. **Keep those two screenshots on your phone and send them in your next message/when uploads become available.**

Ideally they contain the bottom of:

**Baseten → My Ad Centre → “Why you're seeing this ad”**

You've already captured advertiser verification: **Paid for by Baseten Labs, Inc.**

Also, **don't click “See more/fewer … ads,” Like, or customise anything** during this experiment. That would deliberately modify Google's future ad-selection signals and contaminate our observation.

We now have a surprisingly useful sequence:

**Previous video → other unknown ads → Wise at end → start next Big Think video → Specsavers + Baseten two-ad pod.**

And Specsavers and Baseten are radically different categories. That is already evidence against the simplistic model of **“YouTube just shows an ad matching the subject of the current video.”**

The **Baseten targeting explanation is the important missing piece now.** Send those last two screenshots when you can; no need to repeat any of these ten.

Yes. **Before collecting more ads or transcripts, we should define what decision this experiment is supposed to enable.** Otherwise we'll accumulate interesting screenshots without producing anything actionable.

# Goal of the exercise

> **Understand how YouTube/Google advertising actually reaches a viewer across different ad placements and contexts, well enough to decide whether—and how—we can use it as a distribution channel for our own products/services.**

The objective is **not** to reverse-engineer Google's proprietary algorithm. We can't observe enough to do that.

The objective is to extract **actionable distribution knowledge**.

## Outcomes I want us to get

| Outcome | Question we should be able to answer | Why useful |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Placement map** | Where can ads actually appear—pre-roll, mid-roll, post-roll, below/alongside player, feed, etc.? | Different placements may suit different products/messages |
| **2. Selection-signal map** | What does Google disclose as contributing: video, age, location/time, inferred interests, etc.? | Shows what targeting routes potentially exist |
| **3. Context relationship** | How related is the ad to the whole video, exact spoken content, or neither? | Tests whether contextual advertising can reach adjacent audiences |
| **4. Audience relationship** | Do ads appear that look much more related to the viewer's interests than the current content? | Helps investigate audience-based distribution |
| **5. Placement × targeting relationship** | Do different placement types appear to use different disclosed signals? | Potentially very important for campaign design |
| **6. Repetition/cross-video behaviour** | Does the same advertiser/category follow across unrelated videos? | Helps distinguish contextual vs broader audience patterns |
| **7. Advertiser strategy inference** | What might Specsavers, Baseten, Microsoft/Minecraft, Wise etc. be trying to achieve? | Learn from real campaigns rather than generic marketing theory |
| **8. Our distribution strategy** | Which mechanisms could we use for our enterprise/AI products? | **Main commercial outcome** |
| **9. Small campaign design** | What audience/context/creative/placement should we test first and at what budget? | Converts research into action |
| **10. Measurement plan** | What result means Scale / Hold / Stop? | Prevents spending money because ads merely “look promising” |

But there's another outcome that I think is equally important given what has happened in this conversation.

# Outcome 11: improve the way our AI system thinks

This exercise has unexpectedly become a **test case for proactive AI reasoning**.

You've had to point out several missing dimensions:

**ad appeared →** I analysed targeting.

You: *What about the video content?*

**video content →** I looked at chapters.

You: *But Minecraft isn't an interrupting video ad; it's a lower placement.*

**placement →** I corrected the model.

You: *But you don't actually possess the transcript.*

That's extremely useful evidence about a failure mode.

So a second deliverable should be a reusable reasoning protocol:

> **Goal → required evidence → available evidence → capability/knowledge gaps → acquire missing evidence → observations → competing hypotheses → discriminating test → decision value → stop/continue → action.**

We can eventually apply that protocol not merely to advertising, but to **product building, distribution, debugging, business decisions and the multi-AI system you're considering.**

---

# What we should NOT try to achieve

This boundary matters.

We should **not** claim that we're going to determine Google's exact algorithm, auction weights, private user profile, or precisely why an individual advertiser won an auction.

For example:

> “Google says interests + location/time were used.”

is evidence.

But:

> “Google showed Minecraft because it knows Senthil likes games.”

would be an unsupported causal conclusion.

Likewise, even if the transcript contains the word **“challenge”** exactly when Minecraft's **“Brave The Unknown”** creative appears, that's an interesting correlation—not proof Google matched that word.

That's why getting the transcripts is useful, but **we shouldn't become obsessed with individual words** unless repeated observations support that hypothesis.

# The experiment should end in an action

After perhaps **20–30 naturally occurring ad observations**, I don't want us saying:

> “Interesting. Let's collect another 100.”

We should have enough to produce something like:

**YouTube Distribution Experiment v1**

**Product:** one of our AI/enterprise products  
**Buyer:** defined persona  
**Placement:** chosen based on evidence  
**Targeting:** contextual/audience/etc.  
**Creative A/B:** two propositions  
**Landing page:** one measurable conversion  
**Test budget:** deliberately small  
**Success threshold:** predetermined  
**Decision:** Scale / Modify / Stop

Then **our own campaign becomes Experiment 2**.

And that experiment will teach us much more than watching other people's ads because we'll finally have access to the other half of the system: **campaign settings, impressions, CPM/CPV, clicks, conversions, audiences and cost.**

So I would define the exercise in one sentence:

> ### **Observe how Google/YouTube connects viewer + content + context + placement + advertiser, then convert those observations into a cheap, measurable distribution experiment for something we actually want to sell.**

That gives us a stopping condition and prevents this becoming research for research's sake.

Yes. **We absolutely need to distinguish the human contributor from the AI that processed the contribution.** Your example exposes an important weakness in the filename I proposed.

There are actually **three different identities** we may need.

### 1. `SOURCE_ACTOR`
Who generated/provided the real-world observation?

Examples:

`SENTHIL`  
`MADANRAJ`  
`SUBHA`  
`WIFE`  
`DAUGHTER01`

We should preferably use stable contributor IDs rather than full personal names where privacy matters.

### 2. `PROCESSOR`
Which AI/system created the Git artefact?

Examples:

`CHATGPT`  
`CLAUDE`  
`PERPLEXITY`  
`HUMAN`

### 3. `OPERATOR`
Who was actually interacting with that AI account/session?

This is subtly different.

For example:

> Madhanraj sees an advertisement → sends screenshot to **you** → you give it to ChatGPT.

Then:

```text
source_actor: MADANRAJ
operator: SENTHIL
processor: CHATGPT
```

But Madhanraj could directly use ChatGPT himself:

```text
source_actor: MADANRAJ
operator: MADANRAJ
processor: CHATGPT
```

Or your daughter sees something and sends it to you:

```text
source_actor: DAUGHTER01
operator: SENTHIL
processor: CHATGPT
```

That provenance distinction can become extremely important later.

---

# Don't put all three into every filename

This is where I would **not over-engineer the filename**.

If we make filenames:

```text
MAILAB_MADANRAJ_SENTHIL_CHATGPT_YOUTUBE_AD_OBSERVATION...
```

they'll become horrible.

Instead use **two levels of identity**.

### Filename: source actor + processor

For evidence/observation:

```text
<PROJECT>_<SOURCE-ACTOR>_<PROCESSOR>_<TYPE>_<DESCRIPTION>_<TIMESTAMP>
```

Example:

```text
MAILAB_MADANRAJ_CHATGPT_OBSERVATION_BASETEN_20261012_2015.md
```

That tells us immediately:

**MAI-Lab + Madhanraj supplied observation + ChatGPT processed it.**

Inside the file we carry full provenance:

```yaml
project: Market & Attention Intelligence Lab
project_code: MAILAB

source_actor_id: MADANRAJ
operator_actor_id: SENTHIL
processor: CHATGPT

observed_at: 2026-10-12T20:12:00+01:00
processed_at: 2026-10-12T20:15:00+01:00

source_fidelity: VERBATIM
```

That's enough for programming while keeping filenames manageable.

---

# But TURN files are different

For a TURN, **actor means whoever performed that turn**, not necessarily whoever originally observed the advertisement.

Suppose you tell me:

> “Madhanraj sent me these screenshots. Analyse them.”

The Git TURN is yours + mine:

```text
MAILAB_CHATGPT_SENTHIL_TURN_0012_MADANRAJ-AD-OBSERVATION_20261012_2015.md
```

Inside it:

```yaml
turn_actor: SENTHIL
ai_actor: CHATGPT

evidence_source_actor: MADANRAJ
```

This preserves an important distinction:

> **Who said it? Who observed it? Who submitted it? Who analysed it?**

Those are not necessarily the same person.

---

# We should therefore add this to V004

I would formalise a **Provenance Identity Model**:

```text
REAL WORLD
    │
    ▼
SOURCE ACTOR
Who originally observed/created it?
    │
    ▼
OPERATOR
Who submitted/interacted with AI?
    │
    ▼
PROCESSOR
Which AI/system transformed it?
    │
    ▼
REVIEWER(S)
Who later checked/challenged it?
```

Example:

```text
Minecraft ad
     │
     ▼
SENTHIL
observed
     │
     ▼
SENTHIL
submitted
     │
     ▼
CHATGPT
analysed
     │
     ├──► PERPLEXITY reviewed
     │
     └──► CLAUDE challenged
```

Now imagine six months later Claude says:

> “The original observer reported this as a mid-roll.”

We can determine whether **the observer actually said that** or **ChatGPT inferred it incorrectly**.

That exact distinction would have helped with the Minecraft mistake we already encountered.

---

## Contributor registry

We should also create:

```text
contributors/
    README.md
    CONTRIBUTOR_REGISTRY.md
```

But keep it **minimal**.

Something like:

| ID | Role/type | Display label |
|---|---|---|
| SENTHIL | Human | Senthil |
| MADANRAJ | Human | Madhanraj |
| SUBHA | Human | Subha |
| WIFE01 | Human | Family contributor |
| DAUGHTER01 | Human | Family contributor |
| CHATGPT | AI | ChatGPT |
| CLAUDE | AI | Claude |
| PERPLEXITY | AI | Perplexity |

For family members, especially children, **we do not need real names merely for provenance**. Stable pseudonymous IDs are sufficient unless there's a genuine reason otherwise.

And importantly, we should **not store unnecessary personal information** about contributors.

---

## One more distinction: observer vs owner

This will matter when people start contributing.

Madhanraj seeing an advertisement doesn't necessarily mean Madhanraj owns the resulting research record.

So later we may also need:

```yaml
source_actor: MADANRAJ
contribution_scope: research
consent_scope: internal
publication_permission: NOT_GRANTED
```

That becomes important before our future **internal → public promotion gate**.

Someone agreeing:

> “Here is an interesting ad I saw.”

does **not automatically mean**:

> “Publish my viewing behaviour publicly.”

So V004's Public Promotion Protocol should require checking contribution/publication scope.

---

### Therefore the standard becomes

**Filename = enough provenance to identify the artefact quickly.**

**File metadata = complete provenance.**

**Contributor registry = stable identities.**

**Git history = who technically committed/changed the repository.**

Those four shouldn't be confused.

And yes—**this is another genuine V004 improvement discovered before creating MAI-Lab**. This is precisely why I'm glad we haven't rushed into creating the folder tree yet.

Yes. I think you are describing something **larger than the narrow YouTube-targeting experiment I framed earlier**.

What you've been doing—saving the ad, the video/Short where you encountered it, the advertiser landing page, screenshots, and links—is potentially a **continuous market-observation system**. We should preserve that habit rather than narrowing it to “why did Google show me this ad?”

## The broader goal

> **Build a longitudinal library of real-world advertising, content, offers and landing pages, then use AI to discover how markets, messaging, creative styles, products and audience acquisition change over time.**

That can give us several layers of learning.

### 1. What companies are pushing *now*

If we keep observations over months, we can see:

- which companies suddenly start appearing;
- which products they are promoting;
- which offers disappear quickly versus run for months;
- frequency/repetition;
- changes in headline, CTA, video creative and landing page;
- seasonal/time-of-day changes;
- new categories appearing;
- companies repeatedly spending to reach similar audiences.

An ad that you see once is an anecdote.

If **Baseten appears 14 times over six weeks**, with three creatives and two landing pages, that's a completely different signal.

We still cannot infer their actual spend or campaign profitability, but **persistence + creative iteration + landing-page changes** becomes useful competitive intelligence.

---

## 2. Learn advertising by observing the entire funnel

Your old WhatsApp habit actually contained an important insight.

Don't save only:

**Ad screenshot**

Save the chain:

**Content being consumed → exact context/timestamp → ad placement → creative → advertiser → CTA → landing page → offer → conversion mechanism**

For a Short, ideally preserve the **Short URL** too.

For a normal video, preserve the **video URL + transcript + timestamp**.

Then months later we can ask questions that would be impossible from isolated screenshots:

> Which hooks keep recurring in AI-company ads?

> Are technical companies sending people directly to products, books, reports, webinars, demos or email capture?

> Which advertisers changed landing pages but retained the same creative?

> Which ads repeatedly occur around productivity/entrepreneurship/AI/neuroscience content?

> Are “free resource → email → product” funnels becoming more common?

> What video styles repeatedly survive for months?

> What words/hooks/visual structures are being reused across unrelated companies?

That can absolutely feed back into **our own video creation**.

Not by copying their videos, but by discovering patterns such as:

**Hook → curiosity gap → proof → demonstration → CTA**

or

**Problem → surprising claim → education → free asset → lead capture**

and testing those structures ourselves.

---

# The time dimension is especially valuable

You mentioned that campaigns may change over time. **Exactly.**

That's one reason I wouldn't turn this into a fixed “research project” with 20 observations and stop.

There are really **two modes**:

**Experiment mode:** collect enough structured observations to answer a specific question.

**Radar mode:** indefinitely and cheaply preserve interesting ads encountered naturally.

Radar mode shouldn't interrupt your life. When something catches your attention, save it. AI does the classification later.

Over time we can construct something like:

`Advertiser → date → product → creative → placement → source content → targeting explanation → landing page → offer → CTA → recurrence`

Then we gain **history**, not merely examples.

That's substantially more valuable.

---

## There is one thing I would add to your old collection habit

**Capture why *you* noticed it.**

A one-line field:

> **Why I stopped:** technical relevance / surprising hook / visual / product idea / offer / unknown company / repeated advertiser / other.

Because there's another dataset hiding here:

### Your own attention.

After 100 observations we might discover that *you* repeatedly stop for:

- diagrams rather than talking heads;
- technical educational offers;
- “here's the system” messages;
- unusual product demonstrations;
- particular types of headlines.

That doesn't establish what everybody likes.

But it teaches us something about **attention mechanics for one repeatedly observed viewer**, which we can then turn into hypotheses and test against broader audiences.

---

# About what I “already know” internally

There's an important correction to one part of your reasoning.

You're broadly right that advertising fundamentals aren't secret magic. I can explain things like segmentation, positioning, auctions, contextual targeting, creative testing, funnels, attribution, conversion optimisation, remarketing, experimentation, and so forth.

But it isn't accurate to think:

> “ChatGPT contains Google's complete advertising algorithm/training material, but OpenAI decides whether this particular user deserves access to it.”

That's **not how my knowledge works**.

OpenAI describes its models as learning patterns from large amounts of information rather than retaining a database of their training materials. Training sources include publicly available information, licensed/partner data, and information supplied/generated by users, trainers and researchers. After training, I don't have a searchable catalogue saying *“here are the Google-internal documents I was trained on.”* citeturn0search0turn0search1

So I can't say:

> “I was trained on Google's private YouTube Ads ranking manual and here is what it says.”

I don't know that, and I don't have privileged access to Google's internal auction system.

There **are** also things I won't provide because of safety/privacy rules, and there is internal information I don't expose. My raw hidden reasoning, for example, isn't something I can provide verbatim; OpenAI explicitly keeps model chain-of-thought hidden. I *can* provide conclusions, assumptions, evidence, alternatives and concise reasoning summaries. citeturn0search5

But there isn't a general **“ordinary customer versus army versus special customer gets different secret world knowledge”** switch that I can use to unlock proprietary Google advertising knowledge for you.

What I *can* do is arguably more useful for this project:

**general advertising knowledge + Google's published information + live observations + transcripts + creatives + landing pages + longitudinal data + controlled experiments → new conclusions.**

That's genuine reverse engineering from observable behaviour.

---

# And I wouldn't call what you're building “jack of all trades” in the negative sense

There's a difference between:

**knowing a little randomly about 100 subjects**

and

**having enough working knowledge across product + AI + advertising + psychology + content + sales + analytics to connect them.**

The second is **systems-level breadth**.

AI dramatically lowers the cost of crossing domains. You don't need to become a 10-year Google Ads specialist before asking a sophisticated advertising question. I can supply the conceptual scaffolding, research current specifics, and help analyse evidence; specialists can still be brought in when the consequences justify it.

The competitive advantage then isn't merely **how much you know**.

It's:

> **Can you connect observations from different domains into a hypothesis, test it cheaply, learn, and act faster than somebody who sees each domain separately?**

That is exactly why this little YouTube-ad exercise may be worth continuing.

And now we have a clearer design: **don't turn it into homework. Keep collecting naturally as you already did. Preserve richer evidence when something looks interesting. Then periodically let us mine the accumulated observations for patterns and decide which patterns deserve an actual experiment.**

Yes. We can make this **much lighter for you**. You should not become the data-entry operator for this experiment.

Your job should mainly be: **send the YouTube link before watching, and when an ad appears take 2–3 screenshots without clicking away from the ad.** I should do the research and reconstruction afterward.

# Our capture protocol

## A. Before you start a new YouTube video

Send me **only the YouTube URL**.

For example:

> `https://youtu.be/RZIn9tfeQ2I...`

**Don't start playing immediately if convenient.**

I should then independently collect everything I can:

**video title → channel → duration → description → chapters → publication date → transcript availability → transcript if actually accessible → topic/content → other useful public metadata.**

And importantly, I'll explicitly report:

**✅ I have** — things I actually obtained.

**⚠️ Partial** — e.g. chapters/summary but no complete transcript.

**❌ Need from you** — usually YouTube transcript if I cannot retrieve it.

Only then do you supply what's genuinely missing.

That fixes the problem we've just discovered.

---

# B. When an ad appears — don't chase the landing-page link

Your concern about two-ad pods is correct.

If YouTube says something like:

**Ad 1 of 2**

and you click through to investigate Ad 1, we may destroy the natural sequence and never observe Ad 2.

**Preserving the impression is more important than obtaining the landing page at that moment.**

### Screenshot 1 — the ad exactly as it appeared

This is the most important screenshot.

Capture the **whole screen**, like you've already been doing.

Ideally it lets me recover:

- advertiser/brand;
- creative;
- headline;
- CTA;
- visible URL/domain;
- `1 of 2` / `2 of 2`;
- countdown/Skip;
- video progress if visible;
- whether the underlying video is playing;
- placement geometry;
- surrounding YouTube UI.

**Don't crop it.**

The surrounding screen is evidence.

---

## Screenshot 2 — My Ad Centre / ad-information panel

Open the **ⓘ / three dots / My Ad Centre** information **only if doing so doesn't lose the next ad**.

Capture the top portion containing:

**advertiser identity + verified advertiser + country + “ad funded by”**, when available.

Then scroll enough to include:

### **“Why you're seeing this ad”**

This is actually the highest-value part for our targeting research.

Your previous screenshots were excellent because they exposed things such as:

**age / video you're watching / time or general location / estimated interests.**

### Screenshot 3 only when necessary

If **“Why you're seeing this ad” doesn't fit in Screenshot 2**, take one more screenshot after scrolling.

So the normal target is:

> **2 screenshots per ad; maximum 3 when necessary.**

Not ten.

---

# C. When YouTube gives two consecutive ads

This changes the priority.

Suppose:

**Ad 1 of 2 → Ad 2 of 2**

For **Ad 1**, first take **Screenshot 1 only**.

Then **don't click anything likely to navigate away**.

Let Ad 2 arrive.

Take **Screenshot 1 for Ad 2**.

Now, if YouTube still lets you inspect its information safely, capture My Ad Centre.

We may therefore occasionally have:

**Ad 1 = creative evidence only**

**Ad 2 = creative + targeting explanation**

That's completely acceptable.

**Natural sequence > perfect documentation of one impression.**

---

# D. Don't click the advertiser landing page during the impression

I agree with you here too.

If the ad visibly gives us:

**Baseten → baseten.co → Inference Engineering → Download**

I should first try to locate the campaign/landing page myself afterward.

If I find it:

**you do nothing.**

If I can't confidently identify the exact landing page, I'll tell you:

> **Landing page unresolved — next time this creative appears, capture/copy the destination if convenient.**

That makes *you* the fallback rather than the primary researcher.

And if an ad has **no external landing-page link at all**, that's not failed data.

That's itself a useful field:

> **Destination: YouTube-native / no external destination exposed**

because we're studying **ad formats as well as advertisers**.

---

# E. One extra thing I want that costs you almost nothing

When possible, **don't crop or hide the phone status bar**.

Your screenshots already contain clock information.

That lets us preserve approximately:

**22:31 → Ad 1**

**22:32 → targeting panel**

etc.

But one correction to what you said: I have awareness of the conversation's current date/time context, but I shouldn't assume I have a perfect forensic timestamp for every historical event merely because messages appear in sequence. **The phone clock visible inside the screenshot is stronger evidence for when that screenshot was actually captured.**

We should preserve both rather than pretending they're equivalent.

---

# F. Video timestamp matters differently depending on placement

This is another thing **I should infer from the screenshot**, not make you type.

For an interrupting ad:

> Video paused around `18:42` → mid-roll candidate.

For:

> `Sponsored · 1 of 2` before playback → pre-roll/ad pod.

For your Minecraft example:

> Video remains at `2:35 / 1:02:28` while advertisement is shown outside the player.

That's a different placement class.

For something after the content completes:

> post-video/post-roll candidate.

**You shouldn't classify any of those. Send the uncropped screenshot; I'll classify it.**

---

# Therefore your actual workload is tiny

### Before watching

**Send URL.**

Wait for me to say whether I need transcript/content evidence.

### Advertisement appears

**Screenshot full ad.**

If there are two ads, **capture both creatives before investigating**.

### After preserving the creative(s)

Open **My Ad Centre → screenshot advertiser + “Why you're seeing this ad.”**

That's it.

Don't manually type:

advertiser, timestamp, placement, CTA, targeting factors, domain, video title, ad number, etc.

**Those are my job to extract.**

---

# What I should build from each observation

Internally our record becomes something like:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Observation date/time | 10 Oct 2026 ~22:32 |
| Source video | Big Think — Steven Kotler |
| Full transcript | Available / missing |
| Video timestamp | 02:35 |
| Exact transcript around timestamp | captured if available |
| Placement | outside-player/watch-page |
| Interrupts video | No |
| Advertiser | Microsoft |
| Product | Minecraft Dungeons II |
| Creative message | Brave the Unknown |
| Ad sequence | standalone / 1 of 2 / 2 of 2 |
| Destination | Xbox/Minecraft/etc. |
| Google disclosed: age | Yes/No |
| Google disclosed: video | Yes/No |
| Google disclosed: location/time | Yes/No |
| Google disclosed: interests | Yes/No |
| Whole-video semantic relationship | later analysis |
| Moment-level semantic relationship | later analysis |
| Repeated advertiser | count |
| Creative changed? | Yes/No |
| Landing page changed? | Yes/No |
| Our interpretation | hypothesis |
| Confidence | observed/inferred/unknown |

And eventually the interesting part isn't one row.

It's:

**Baseten × 8 appearances**  
**Wise × 5**  
**Microsoft × 12**  
**Specsavers × 9**

across:

**different videos × different times × different placements × different creatives × different landing pages × different disclosed targeting signals.**

Now we have the longitudinal **advertising radar** you were describing.

---

## One more improvement: don't interrupt normal viewing for mediocre ads

We shouldn't make every YouTube session into work.

I suggest a simple rule:

**New advertiser → capture.**

**Known advertiser but new creative/product/placement → capture.**

**Known advertiser repeating unchanged → one full-screen screenshot is enough** so we increment recurrence/time/context without reopening every panel.

**Something unusually interesting → capture everything.**

That gives us longitudinal frequency without drowning ourselves in duplicate screenshots.

So from your **next YouTube video onward**, just send me the URL first. **I should take responsibility for determining what I can obtain myself and tell you exactly what evidence—if any—is missing before you start watching.**

**Yes. That is the more fundamental miss.**

Before I started comparing **Wise → Specsavers → Baseten → Minecraft**, I should have performed an **evidence-availability check**.

I should have reasoned:

> “We're trying to determine whether ads relate to video content. Therefore I need the content of *both videos*, preferably timestamped transcripts. I cannot assume I can directly watch/listen to arbitrary YouTube videos from the URL. First try to retrieve reliable public transcripts; if I cannot retrieve them completely, ask Senthil for the transcripts.”

In fact, for the **second video** I can now find an indexed transcript, including Big Think's own transcript page, so I don't need to make you provide that one. citeturn0search0turn0search3

But I **haven't established a reliable transcript for the first video (`lgErkgdMrmk`)**. Searching its ID did not produce the equivalent transcript in my results. So rather than pretending I understand its complete content from metadata, **I should ask you for that first video's timestamped transcript**.

## The reasoning protocol needs another layer

What you've exposed isn't merely “AI should think of more possibilities.” It's **self-awareness about evidence and tool limitations**.

Before analysis I should automatically run:

**GOAL → REQUIRED EVIDENCE → WHAT I ACTUALLY HAVE → WHAT I CAN RETRIEVE → WHAT'S MISSING → ASK USER ONLY FOR THE MISSING PART → ANALYSE**

Applied here:

| Needed | Status |
|---|---|
| First video's transcript | ❌ **Need from you / another reliable source** |
| First video's ad observations | Partial — your screenshots + recollection |
| Second video's transcript | ✅ Publicly retrievable |
| Second video's exact content around 2:35 | ✅ Retrievable |
| Ad placement type | ✅ Screenshots |
| Google's “Why this ad” | ✅ For several impressions |
| Exact advertiser targeting configuration | ❌ Not visible to us |
| Auction competitors/bids | ❌ Not visible |
| Why a particular ad won beyond disclosed factors | ❌ Cannot know directly |

That table should have existed **before conclusions**.

### So please send me the transcript for the **first video `lgErkgdMrmk`**

Preferably **timestamped**, if you have it. You **do not need to send the second transcript** unless your YouTube transcript differs from the public version I found.

Then I'll correlate the first and second videos against the ads at **three levels**:

**Video-level context** — what the whole video is about.

**Moment-level context** — what was being discussed when an ad appeared, *where that makes sense for the placement*.

**Placement/targeting context** — pre-roll, mid-roll, post-roll, lower/watch-feed unit + Google's disclosed selection factors.

And importantly, **“unknown” stays unknown**. We won't convert correlation into a targeting claim.

---

This also gives us a better answer to your larger question about making ChatGPT/Claude/Perplexity more useful.

Don't merely instruct them:

> “Think harder and be proactive.”

Give the system a permanent **epistemic preflight**:

**1. What is the user's actual goal?  
2. What evidence would ideally answer it?  
3. What evidence do I currently possess?  
4. What can I independently obtain?  
5. What can I *not* access or verify?  
6. What missing evidence has the highest decision value?  
7. Obtain/ask for that evidence before drawing conclusions.  
8. Generate competing explanations.  
9. Rank them by evidence, not plausibility.  
10. Ask: will further investigation change the next action? If no → STOP and ACT.**

That last step prevents the system you fear: **three clever AIs endlessly debating while nothing gets built.**

So yes: **self-awareness of missing evidence should come *before* expansive thinking.** Otherwise an AI can perform sophisticated reasoning on an incomplete representation of the situation—which is exactly what happened here.

Yes. We should now stop treating this as an informal sequence of screenshots and establish it as a **real evolving project**.

And I would **not** define the project as “understand YouTube ads.” That's too small. YouTube ads are our **first observable data source**.

# Project: Market & Attention Intelligence System — v0.1

**Working date:** 10 October 2026  
**Current phase:** Discovery / evidence collection  
**Status:** Project definition established after initial exploratory observations

---

## 1. Vision

> **Build a continuously learning market-intelligence system that observes how companies attract attention, position products, advertise, create content, construct offers and convert audiences—and turns those observations into actionable knowledge for our own products, content and distribution.**

The important phrase is **continuously learning**.

We're not trying to take a Google Ads course and finish it.

We're building an evidence base that can answer questions such as:

**What's changing in the market? What are companies repeatedly promoting? What messages survive? What catches attention? Where are advertisements appearing? What content surrounds them? What happens after the click? What patterns persist over weeks/months? And which of those patterns should we actually test ourselves?**

---

# 2. Mission

Our immediate mission is narrower:

> **Capture naturally occurring YouTube advertising and its surrounding context with minimal manual effort, reconstruct the advertiser → creative → placement → targeting signals → content context → landing page → offer journey, and learn from patterns over time.**

YouTube is **Phase 1**, not necessarily the final boundary.

Later this architecture could accept:

Instagram/Reels → LinkedIn → websites → newsletters → Google Search ads → Shorts → product launches → landing pages → other channels.

But **we do not expand there now.**

We first prove the method on YouTube.

---

# 3. What are we actually trying to produce?

There are **three outputs**, not one.

## Output A — Knowledge

Build our understanding of:

**Advertising + attention + content + positioning + offers + funnels + targeting + distribution + changing market behaviour.**

This addresses your “expand our knowledge” objective.

Instead of learning every field from scratch through courses, we combine:

**real observations + established theory + current public information + AI analysis.**

---

## Output B — Actionable intelligence for our own work

Knowledge alone isn't sufficient.

Eventually the system should be able to say:

> “We've observed this pattern repeatedly. It may be relevant to Product X. Here's a £50/£100/£500 experiment that would test whether it works for us.”

Or:

> “These technical companies aren't primarily advertising their enterprise product directly. Several are advertising educational assets that capture interested users first. Consider testing that acquisition structure.”

Or:

> “This video structure repeatedly appears across unrelated advertisers. Let's test the structure in three of our videos.”

That's where the research becomes commercially useful.

---

## Output C — potentially a product

**But I would NOT declare today that we're building a commercial product.**

That's premature.

The progression should be:

**Personal practice → structured dataset → repeatable methodology → useful internal system → automation → only then ask whether others have the same problem → potential product.**

If we discover that this system gives us unusual market intelligence with little effort, *then* there may be a product:

> **AI Market Radar / Advertising Intelligence / Attention Intelligence**

But we shouldn't invent a SaaS because we collected five ads.

**Productisation is a hypothesis, not the current goal.**

---

# 4. The project has two parallel tracks

This is important because our conversation evolved.

### Track 1 — Market/advertising intelligence

Study the external world.

### Track 2 — AI reasoning intelligence

Study **how our AIs reason about the external world**.

The second track emerged accidentally because you repeatedly caught reasoning gaps in my analysis.

That is potentially as valuable as the advertising research.

---

# 5. How the project evolved

Let's preserve this because you specifically don't want us rewriting history later.

### Stage 0 — Your old habit

Long before this experiment, you already had a habit of saving interesting advertising material in WhatsApp:

**creative/video → screenshot → link → landing page**

with the intention that it might be useful later.

There was no formal schema or automated analysis.

But the underlying instinct was correct:

> **Preserve interesting market evidence now because future analysis may reveal patterns that aren't visible from one observation.**

That is effectively the origin of this project.

---

## Stage 1 — “Why am I seeing these ads?”

We started with ads appearing during your YouTube viewing.

Examples accumulated:

**Wise → Specsavers → Baseten → Minecraft Dungeons II.**

Initial question:

> Why is YouTube showing these advertisements to me?

This produced our first proposed goal:

### Goal v0.1
**Understand YouTube ad targeting.**

Useful, but too narrow.

---

# 6. First expansion — distribution

We then recognised that understanding targeting has commercial value.

If companies can reach relevant people even when those people aren't explicitly searching for their product:

> Could we use those mechanisms to distribute our products?

That produced:

### Goal v0.2
**Understand how YouTube connects viewer + content + context + advertiser sufficiently to design our own advertising/distribution experiment.**

Better.

But still incomplete.

---

# 7. Second expansion — market intelligence

You then pointed out something I had underweighted:

Why study only **why the ad reached you?**

We're simultaneously seeing:

**which companies advertise → what they're selling → how frequently → creative → messaging → video → CTA → landing page → offer → how it changes over time.**

That changed the project significantly.

### Goal v0.3 — CURRENT

> **Use naturally encountered advertising as a continuous sensor of the market and convert accumulated observations into knowledge and actionable experiments for content, products and distribution.**

This is where we stand now.

---

# 8. What evidence have we already collected?

Our first exploratory observations include at least:

| Advertiser/product | What we learned |
|---|---|
| **Wise** | Ad observed at/around end of first viewing sequence; initial placement interpretation needs careful evidence |
| **Specsavers** | Start-of-video ad; advertiser identity; Scottish eligibility messaging; Google disclosed age + current video + time/general location + inferred interests |
| **Baseten** | Second of two start ads; Inference Engineering educational asset; Google disclosed age + current video + time/general location; interests not listed |
| **Minecraft Dungeons II** | Advertisement displayed outside/below video rather than interrupting playback; Google disclosure showed time/general location + inferred interests in captured panel |

These aren't enough to establish general rules.

But they were enough to expose what our data model needs.

---

# 9. Mistakes we made — preserve these

These are not embarrassing project history. They're **requirements discovery**.

### Mistake 1 — treating all ads as the same placement

I initially interpreted Minecraft around `2:35` as though it were an interrupting video ad.

You corrected:

> It is shown in the lower area while the video continues.

**Lesson:** placement must be an explicit observation.

---

### Mistake 2 — analysing video context without possessing the transcript

I used chapter information as though it gave sufficient resolution about what was actually being said.

You challenged:

> How will you know what word was used?

Correct.

**Lesson:**

`Video URL ≠ video access`

`Chapter ≠ transcript`

`Summary ≠ exact spoken content`

The system needs an **evidence-availability check before reasoning.**

---

### Mistake 3 — not asking for the first video's transcript

Once our hypothesis became:

> Is advertisement related to video content?

I should automatically have realised:

**I need the content of both videos.**

Instead you had to point this out.

**Lesson:** derive required evidence from the hypothesis before analysing.

---

### Mistake 4 — making you do research I could potentially do

You shouldn't have to manually capture every landing page if I can identify it afterward from:

**advertiser + creative + CTA + visible domain + web research.**

**Lesson:** human captures ephemeral evidence; AI reconstructs persistent/public evidence.

That's a very important division of labour.

---

### Mistake 5 — prematurely narrowing the project's purpose

I proposed collecting perhaps 20–30 observations and then running an advertising experiment.

You pointed out the longitudinal value:

**repetition → creative changes → companies → campaigns → landing pages → market evolution.**

Correct.

**Lesson:** there are both **bounded experiments** and a **permanent low-cost radar**.

---

# 10. Human–AI division of labour

This should become a project principle.

## You capture what disappears.

Examples:

**the actual ad impression, sequence 1-of-2/2-of-2, UI placement, My Ad Centre explanation.**

Those can disappear within seconds.

## AI retrieves what persists.

I should attempt:

**video metadata → transcript → company → advertiser → product → campaign → landing page → company information → advertising mechanics → historical/contextual research.**

Only if something important cannot be obtained should I ask you.

That's much more scalable.

---

# 11. Capture protocol v1

Your burden should remain extremely small.

### Before watching

Send:

> **YouTube URL**

I investigate it first.

I return:

**AVAILABLE / PARTIAL / MISSING**

especially transcript availability.

If I genuinely need the transcript, I ask.

Then you watch normally.

### When an advertisement appears

First priority:

> **Full-screen screenshot of the advertisement.**

If:

**1 of 2**

capture it and **don't navigate away**.

Then:

**2 of 2 → screenshot.**

Preserve the natural sequence first.

Afterward, when possible:

> **My Ad Centre → advertiser identity + Why you're seeing this ad**

Usually one or two additional screenshots.

**Don't click the advertiser merely to obtain its landing page while doing so risks destroying the ad sequence.**

I'll attempt to reconstruct the landing page later.

---

# 12. What gets stored per observation

Eventually we should stop holding this only in conversational memory and create an actual dataset.

Each observation should conceptually contain:

### Source context
Date/time  
Source URL  
Video/channel  
Duration  
Transcript availability  
Exact video timestamp  
Transcript around timestamp

### Advertisement
Advertiser  
Product  
Creative  
Headline  
CTA  
Visible domain  
Sequence position  
Placement  
Interrupted playback?  
Duration if applicable

### Google's explanation
Age  
Video watched  
Time/general location  
Estimated interests  
Other disclosed signals

### Funnel
Landing page  
Offer  
Price/free  
Lead capture  
CTA  
Conversion mechanism

### Analysis
Contextual relationship  
Audience relationship hypothesis  
Creative pattern  
Repeated advertiser?  
Repeated creative?  
Changed landing page?  
Confidence  
Unknowns

---

# 13. Repetition becomes a first-class signal

This is one of your important additions.

One appearance:

> observation.

Five appearances:

> pattern candidate.

Twenty appearances over three months:

> potentially meaningful persistence.

And we shouldn't merely count advertiser.

We count:

**Advertiser × product × creative × placement × destination × time × source context.**

Because:

> Baseten appeared 12 times

is less informative than:

> Baseten appeared 12 times, using four creatives, but repeatedly sent users to the same educational asset.

That starts telling a story.

---

# 14. We need snapshots, not just URLs

This follows directly from your time-change observation.

Landing pages change.

Ads disappear.

Offers expire.

Companies reposition.

Therefore a URL alone isn't enough.

Where practical, we eventually preserve:

**URL + observed date + screenshot/snapshot + extracted proposition.**

Then we can compare:

**October → November → January**

and detect changes.

That's actual longitudinal competitive intelligence.

---

# 15. Our learning loop

The system should eventually operate like:

**OBSERVE**

↓  

**PRESERVE**

↓  

**ENRICH**

AI finds everything it reasonably can.

↓

**CLASSIFY**

placement, company, product, message, funnel, etc.

↓

**CONNECT**

find previous appearances and related companies/patterns.

↓

**HYPOTHESISE**

why might this pattern exist?

↓

**CHALLENGE**

what alternative explanation fits?

↓

**PRIORITISE**

does resolving this matter?

↓

**TEST**

research or run our own experiment.

↓

**LEARN**

update knowledge.

↓

**ACT**

change content/product/distribution.

That last arrow matters enormously.

Otherwise we're building a museum of screenshots.

---

# 16. Measures of success

We shouldn't measure project success by:

> Number of screenshots collected.

Instead there are maturity levels.

| Level | Capability | Approx. vision progress* |
|---|---|---:|
| **0** | Random screenshots | 0–5% |
| **1** | Structured observations | 10% |
| **2** | Searchable historical dataset | 20% |
| **3** | Recurrence/pattern detection | 35% |
| **4** | Creative + funnel intelligence | 50% |
| **5** | Generates useful hypotheses | 60% |
| **6** | Recommends our experiments | 70% |
| **7** | Experiments produce measurable learning | 80% |
| **8** | Learning changes product/content/distribution decisions | 90% |
| **9** | Mostly automated continuous intelligence loop | **100% of current vision** |

\*These percentages are **project-management markers**, not scientifically measurable percentages.

### Where are we now?

I'd put us around:

> **~10% — moving from Level 0 to Level 1.**

That's not because we've only done 10% of the work literally.

We've discovered:

**the vision + first observations + important failure modes + basic schema + capture protocol.**

But we haven't yet built the durable dataset, analysis pipeline or feedback loop.

---

# 17. Near-term milestones

We shouldn't jump straight to software.

### Milestone 1 — prove capture

**Now → next ~10 useful observations**

Test whether our capture protocol works without disrupting your normal viewing.

Success:

> You don't feel like a research assistant.

---

### Milestone 2 — prove enrichment

I should demonstrate that from your minimal screenshots I can reconstruct substantial information:

**company → product → landing page → offer → source-video context → disclosed targeting → previous appearances.**

Success:

> AI does most of the work.

---

### Milestone 3 — prove longitudinal value

After enough natural observations:

Find at least a few patterns that **wouldn't have been obvious from one screenshot**.

That's critical.

If accumulated history tells us nothing new, the project isn't valuable.

---

### Milestone 4 — convert learning into action

Take **one discovered pattern** and use it.

For example:

**video format**, **hook**, **lead magnet**, **landing-page structure**, **targeting hypothesis**, or **distribution approach**.

Create our own small test.

---

### Milestone 5 — measure

Did it improve:

**attention → engagement → lead → conversion → learning?**

If yes, the intelligence loop has demonstrated value.

---

# 18. Only then consider building a product

At that stage we ask:

> Is this only valuable to us?

or:

> Would founders, marketers, agencies, creators or product teams pay for this intelligence?

If the second becomes plausible, *then* we investigate a product.

The product might ultimately be something quite different from what we're imagining today.

We should let evidence reveal it.

---

# 19. The second project hidden inside this project

I don't want to lose this.

You've repeatedly asked:

> **Why didn't the AI think of that itself?**

So alongside Market Intelligence, we're accumulating examples of **AI reasoning failures**:

- didn't establish required evidence;
- didn't recognise inaccessible evidence;
- confused placement types;
- prematurely inferred context;
- didn't seek adjacent evidence;
- put unnecessary work on human;
- narrowed the goal too soon.

These become requirements for the **proactive multi-AI reasoning architecture** we've been discussing.

Therefore this project gives us **two assets simultaneously**:

### Asset A
**Market & Attention Intelligence**

### Asset B
**Evidence about how a genuinely useful proactive AI should reason**

Those may eventually intersect.

---

# 20. Project charter — v0.1

I'll freeze today's state conceptually as:

> **VISION:** Continuously understand how markets attract attention, communicate value and convert audiences, and transform that knowledge into better products, content and distribution.
>
> **MISSION:** Begin with naturally occurring YouTube advertising and build a low-friction evidence → enrichment → pattern → hypothesis → experiment → action loop.
>
> **CURRENT GOAL:** Establish reliable capture and enrichment before automating or productising.
>
> **HUMAN ROLE:** Capture ephemeral evidence naturally encountered.
>
> **AI ROLE:** Research, enrich, connect, challenge, analyse and identify the next highest-value action.
>
> **CURRENT PHASE:** Discovery / Level 1.
>

>
> **LONG-TERM DELIVERABLE:** A continuously improving market/attention intelligence capability that materially improves our content, product and distribution decisions.
>
> **PRODUCT STATUS:** **Not yet a product. Productisation remains a future hypothesis.**

And I would add one governing rule above everything:

> ### **We don't collect because data might someday be interesting. We preserve low-cost evidence, and the accumulated evidence must eventually change a decision, create an experiment, improve an outcome, or teach us something we couldn't otherwise see.**

That gives this exercise a meaningful destination rather than turning it into another archive of information.

Yes — **this is a second mistake in my analysis.** I treated every screenshot as if we were studying one generic object called “a YouTube ad.” We actually need **two independent dimensions**:

> **WHY was this ad selected?**  
> **WHERE/HOW was this ad presented?**

Your Minecraft screenshot is **not a video-interrupting mid-roll ad**. The Big Think video remains visible at **2:35 / 1:02:28**, while the sponsored Minecraft unit is displayed **outside/below/alongside the player** in the mobile watch experience.

Google explicitly documents ads **outside the video player**, including **Watch feed ads** below the player on mobile and **Watch-While ads** displayed alongside a video without pausing it. Google separately documents in-stream ads that actually play before/during/after the video. citeturn0search4turn0search6

So **I should not have called 2:35 “the point where the Minecraft ad interrupted the video.” It didn't.**

## We need to rebuild the experiment properly

From now on, every ad observation needs this structure:

| Dimension | What we record |
|---|---|
| **Placement** | pre-roll / mid-roll / post-roll / watch-page-feed / watch-while / other |
| **Did content stop?** | Yes / No |
| **Position** | start / video timestamp / end / persistent alongside |
| **Advertiser** | Specsavers, Baseten, Minecraft, Wise… |
| **Creative/product** | eye test / inference book / game / money transfer |
| **Google's disclosed signals** | age / video / location-time / inferred interests |
| **Video context** | video overall topic |
| **Local context** | what was being discussed around that moment, *only when placement makes that relevant* |
| **Hypotheses** | contextual / audience / geographic / remarketing / broad campaign etc. |
| **Confidence** | observed vs inferred |

This also changes how we interpret the earlier evidence.

### What we currently have

**Specsavers and Baseten:** these were actual video ads at the **start of the previous Big Think video** — an **ad pod (1 of 2 / 2 of 2)**. Google says two back-to-back video ads can form an ad pod on long-form content. citeturn0search4

**Wise:** you reported it at the **end of the previous video**. So provisionally **post-roll**, although we should label this *user-observed post-video placement* unless the UI itself proves the exact ad format.

**Minecraft:** fundamentally different. **Outside-player/watch-page advertising while the Big Think video was at 2:35**, not a mid-roll interruption.

And Google's disclosure for Minecraft says **time/general location + inferred interests**; importantly, in what you've captured, it doesn't say **“the video that you're watching.”**

That combination makes the Minecraft example much less useful for testing **“did the exact discussion at 2:35 trigger this ad?”** than I suggested previously.

---

# The bigger issue you're pointing at is more important

You're effectively saying:

> *Why do I have to keep supplying the next reasoning dimension?*

That's the problem.

First you had to tell me:

**“Check the video's content against the ad.”**

Then:

**“But this wasn't an interrupting video ad; it was below the video.”**

Those aren't obscure details. They're dimensions I should generate from the evidence myself.

The desired reasoning isn't simply **“think more.”**

It is:

### **Before concluding, enumerate the dimensions that could change the conclusion.**

For this investigation, I should automatically have generated:

**placement × timing × video context × advertiser × creative × Google's disclosed targeting signals × account/audience signals × geography × auction × repetition across videos.**

Then ask:

> Which of those dimensions can we actually observe?

And:

> Which missing observation would most change our conclusion?

That is much stronger than endlessly brainstorming.

---

## But I don't want to solve this by making three AIs debate everything

You correctly identified the danger:

**too nosy → too many possibilities → confusion → debate → no action.**

Consensus isn't sufficient by itself.

The better controller is:

> **Does this additional reasoning have a reasonable chance of changing our decision or next action?**

For example:

**“Was Minecraft below the video or interrupting it?”**

**HIGH VALUE.** It fundamentally changes our interpretation. Investigate.

**“Was the exact sentence at 2:35 semantically related to Minecraft?”**

Now **LOWER VALUE**, because we discovered this wasn't an interrupting mid-roll and Google's disclosed Minecraft reasons don't mention the current video.

**“Can a technical B2B product like Baseten reach someone through an in-stream YouTube placement while they're consuming adjacent/non-obvious content?”**

**HIGH VALUE for our distribution goal.** Investigate deeply.

That's the mechanism I think we want to build into how **ChatGPT + Claude + Perplexity** collaborate:

**Expand → challenge → rank by decision value → investigate top few → stop → act.**

Not:

**Expand → expand → debate → consensus → expand again.**

And there's one more thing I should now do differently: **don't make you continue manually collecting screenshots indefinitely.** We already have enough to design a proper small experiment. The next step should be to define perhaps **10–20 naturally occurring ad impressions**, what fields we record, and what would confirm/refute each targeting hypothesis. Then your normal YouTube watching generates the dataset without turning you into my research assistant.

That gets us closer to what you're actually asking for: **AI that notices the next useful question itself, while also knowing when to stop thinking and move the work forward.**

Yes. **Your additions justify a V004**, rather than silently modifying V003.

I checked the actual AT Life OS recovery branch. V003 already has immutable actor-owned turns, source fidelity, raw/derived/intelligence separation, concurrency rules, promotion chain, human-burden gate, and an end-of-page audit. fileciteturn3file0L1-L2 But it **does not yet formalise** several things you just identified: README-per-folder, universal standalone filenames, repository-creation protocol, explicit internal→public promotion criteria, or a daily/session digest.

So we should evolve it deliberately.

# Git Governance V004 — proposed additions

## 1. Every folder explains itself

I agree strongly with this.

**No meaningful folder should be created empty.** When we create a directory, create its `README.md` at the same time explaining:

**purpose → what belongs here → what does not → source/derived status → naming convention → relationship to parent/child folders → examples where useful.**

That solves exactly the “new page/new AI doesn't know why this folder exists” problem.

It also means Git can actually retain the directory without `.gitkeep`.

---

## 2. Every important file must survive separation from its folder

Your reasoning is sound.

A downloaded file called:

`analysis.md`

is nearly useless six months later.

So V004 should define a **Standalone File Identity Standard**.

I suggest:

```text
<PROJECT>_<ACTOR-AI>_<TYPE>_<DESCRIPTION>_V<NNN>_<YYYYMMDD_HHMM>.<ext>
```

Example:

```text
MAIL_CHATGPT_PROTOCOL_REPOSITORY-CREATION_V001_20261010_2245.md
```

or a research artefact:

```text
MAIL_PERPLEXITY_ANALYSIS_YOUTUBE-AD-PLACEMENTS_V001_20261011_0930.md
```

Human contribution:

```text
MAIL_MADANRAJ_OBSERVATION_YOUTUBE-ADS_V001_20261012_2015.md
```

The **filename itself carries provenance** even when detached from Git.

For immutable TURN files, we retain sequence as well:

```text
MAIL_CHATGPT_SENTHIL_TURN_0007_AD-CAPTURE-PROTOCOL_20261010_2245.md
```

We should use UTC-offset-aware time **inside file metadata**, while filenames remain filesystem-safe.

---

# 3. Standard file header

Every governed Markdown file gets a machine-readable-ish header:

```yaml
project: Market & Attention Intelligence Lab
project_code: MAIL
document_type: protocol
title: Repository Creation Protocol
version: 001
actor: ChatGPT
created: 2026-10-10T22:45:00+01:00
source_fidelity: VERBATIM
status: draft
supersedes: null
```

Then if somebody downloads only that file, **identity remains both in filename and content**.

That's intentional duplication.

---

# 4. Repository Creation Protocol

This should become a reusable protocol, not something specific to MAI-Lab.

Before creating any future project, the AI must ask:

> **Are there actually two conceptual repositories here—internal/private working evidence and external/public/product output?**

But that does **not** mean automatically create two repos.

Default:

### Internal/private first.

It can contain:

raw evidence → incomplete reasoning → disagreements → mistakes → private context → experiments → abandoned hypotheses.

Public/external repository remains a **potential promotion target**.

---

# 5. When does a public repository get created?

We need an explicit **Public Promotion Gate**.

Don't create the external repository merely because the project sounds publishable.

Create/promote only when there is an identifiable external audience **and** an actual artefact worth publishing, with privacy/IP/security review, source/provenance review, evidence sufficient for its claims, internal-only context removed, documentation usable without private history, and an explicit human decision to publish.

So:

```text
PRIVATE WORKBENCH
      ↓
Evidence
      ↓
Learning
      ↓
Validated output
      ↓
PUBLIC-PROMOTION REVIEW
      ↓
APPROVED?
   ↙       ↘
 NO        YES
 ↓          ↓
remain      create/update
internal    external repo
```

And importantly:

**public is generated/promoted from selected internal knowledge.**

We never simply flip the internal repository from private to public.

---

# 6. Daily/session digest

I agree with your idea, but I wouldn't call it merely `CHANGELOG`, because that term usually means product/version changes.

I'd call it:

## **WORKLOG**

Example:

```text
worklog/
  README.md
  2026/
    10/
      MAIL_CHATGPT_WORKLOG_20261010.md
```

That day's file answers quickly:

> What happened today?

It contains:

**turns created → evidence added → decisions changed → hypotheses added/removed → Learn/Unlearn/Relearn → unresolved disagreements → next return point.**

It links to individual immutable turns.

So tomorrow you **don't have to read 27 TURN files** just to remember where we reached.

---

# 7. CHANGELOG still has a different purpose

We should have both eventually:

**WORKLOG** = what happened during work.

**CHANGELOG** = meaningful changes to project/protocol/methodology versions.

For example:

> `Git TURN V003 → V004`

belongs in CHANGELOG.

> “Analysed Specsavers and discovered placement classification problem”

belongs in WORKLOG.

That distinction will become extremely useful later.

---

# 8. Protocols themselves get their own folder

Rather than throwing standards everywhere:

```text
protocol/
│
├── README.md
│
├── git-turn/
│   └── README.md
│
├── repository-creation/
│   └── README.md
│
├── page-closure/
│   └── README.md
│
├── file-standard/
│   └── README.md
│
├── evidence/
│   └── README.md
│
└── public-promotion/
    └── README.md
```

Versioned protocol documents live inside their appropriate directories.

This satisfies your requirement that a **standardised concept gets a parent/subfolder of its own** rather than becoming random files at root.

---

# 9. Page Closure Protocol

V003 already contains an **End-of-page audit**: verify durable TURN evidence, recover missing turns honestly, reconcile state/decisions/open questions/disagreements/evidence, preserve the exact return point, and create a short bootstrap handover. fileciteturn3file0L2-L2

V004 should promote that from a paragraph into a standalone protocol:

### PAGE CLOSURE

Before leaving a substantial chat/page:

**TURN completeness → evidence completeness → source fidelity → state reconciliation → decision changes → Learn/Unlearn/Relearn → disagreements → worklog update → exact return point → Git commit verification → bootstrap handover.**

That directly addresses your “every page has a lifespan” point.

The next AI/page shouldn't depend on the previous model still remembering.

---

# 10. And every repository root gets an AI bootstrap

AT Life OS already has `AGENTS.md` at root alongside README and its protocol/evidence/state/turn directories. fileciteturn1file0L1-L2

For MAI-Lab, the root should therefore tell ChatGPT/Claude/Perplexity:

> **STOP before working. Read README → AGENTS → current state → applicable protocol → latest worklog → latest handover.**

This is particularly important when Perplexity comes in later and says:

> “I have another hypothesis.”

We want that contribution.

But it must **add a sourced hypothesis**, not rewrite our existing conclusion as though the previous evidence never existed.

---

# Therefore V004 becomes bigger than “Git TURN”

I would actually rename the umbrella:

## **Git Work Continuity Protocol V004**

with components:

**Repository Creation Protocol**  
**Folder README Protocol**  
**Standalone File Standard**  
**Git TURN Protocol**  
**Evidence/Fidelity Protocol**  
**Worklog Protocol**  
**Page Closure Protocol**  
**Public Promotion Protocol**

The **TURN protocol remains one component** rather than trying to stuff everything into TURN.

That's cleaner architecture.

---

## One thing I would change from my previous answer

I proposed project abbreviation **MAI-Lab / MAIL**.

For filenames, don't use `MAIL`. That's too easily confused with email.

Use:

### `MAILAB`

Therefore:

```text
MAILAB_CHATGPT_SENTHIL_TURN_0001_PROJECT-FORMATION_20261010_....md
```

Repository remains:

`market-attention-intelligence-lab`

Human name remains:

**Market & Attention Intelligence Lab**

Project code:

**MAILAB**

---

## Next action

**Don't create the folder tree manually yet.**

Create only the **empty private GitHub repository**:

`market-attention-intelligence-lab`

Then give me the repository URL.

At that point, before we resume YouTube/ad collection, we'll bootstrap it under **Git Work Continuity Protocol V004**, including README files **at folder creation time**, and today's conversation becomes the initial evidence/turn history rather than being lost inside this chat.

That is the right point to establish the standard once, because **the sixth Git-governed project should inherit V004 rather than us reinventing this again.** memcite

Yes. **For the next YouTube ad, don't skip it immediately.** We can capture enough evidence to understand *why that exact ad reached you*.

### When the next ad appears

Please do these, in this order:

1. **Screenshot the ad itself** — like you did for Wise. Make sure the advertiser/company name, **Sponsored** label, and ad message are visible.
2. **Tap the ⓘ beside “Sponsored”** (or the three-dot menu if YouTube shows that instead).
3. **Screenshot the first page that opens.**
4. Look for **“Why this ad?”**, **“About this advertiser”**, or similar. Open **Why this ad?**
5. **Screenshot the entire explanation.** If it scrolls, take 2–3 screenshots so we don't miss anything.
6. If it shows targeting factors such as **location, age, interests, activity, or the content you're watching**, capture those too.
7. **Don't change any ad settings yet.** We want to observe the system in its current state first.

You **do not need to click “Visit advertiser” or “Learn more.”** We're investigating Google's ad-selection mechanism, not the advertiser's landing page.

Also tell me approximately **where in the video it appeared** (for example, `12:40`) and the **real clock time**. I'll compare each ad rather than assuming every ad is caused by the video.

If we capture **3–5 consecutive ads**, including apparently unrelated ones, we'll have a much better dataset: **ad → advertiser → message → position → Google's stated reason → possible targeting mechanism.** Then we can use that evidence for the advertising/distribution discussion we were having earlier.

Yes. **This is exactly the extra step I should have taken myself.** You gave me the video URL, and instead of treating the ad screenshots as an isolated ad-analysis problem, I should have asked:

> **What exactly was being discussed at the instant this ad appeared, and could that context plausibly relate to the ad?**

I searched the video now, and we can reconstruct that context surprisingly well.

## 1. I can access substantial content for this video

Your URL is Big Think's **“The science of effortlessness: How to activate flow | Steven Kotler: Full Interview”**, duration about **1:02:29**. I found a detailed indexed version with chapters/content, plus transcript material elsewhere. citeturn0search0turn0search6

And your screenshot gives us something extremely useful:

**Minecraft Dungeons II ad appeared at approximately `2:35 / 1:02:28`.**

The chapter structure is:

| Video time | Content |
|---|---|
| 00:00 | Introducing Steven Kotler |
| 00:11 | Biology of our brains |
| **00:35** | **Psychology's “outside-in” blind spot** |
| **02:35 ← YOUR AD** | **inside this section** |
| 03:45 | Brain works in networks |
| 06:35 | Four performance pillars |
| 07:40 | Flow's sweet spot |
| 08:49 | What is flow? |
| 15:00 | 22 triggers that spark flow |
| 19:00 | Challenge-skills balance |
| 24:16 | Intrinsic motivation |
| 31:50 | Flow as a focusing skill |
| 37:39 | Flow and peak performance |

citeturn0search0

So the Minecraft ad happened **during the psychology/neurobiology setup**, *before the video had even reached its detailed discussion of flow*.

---

# 2. Now look at Google's explanation for Minecraft

This screenshot is particularly useful.

Google says information used to show you this ad included:

> **“The time of day or your general location (such as your country or city)”**

and

> **“Google's estimation of your interests, based on your activity while you were signed in to Google.”**

Notice what's missing.

### Google does NOT list:

**“The video that you're watching.”**

That's different from both earlier ads.

Our evidence now looks like this:

| Ad | Current video listed by Google? | Estimated interests listed? | Location/time? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Specsavers | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Baseten | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Minecraft Dungeons II** | **❌** | **✅** | ✅ |

That is a very useful natural experiment.

## Therefore, for Minecraft:

I currently see **little evidence that the subject matter at 2:35 caused this particular ad.**

The ad appears while Steven Kotler is discussing psychology/neurobiology, whereas Google itself **doesn't list the current video as information used for this impression**.

Instead, Google's disclosed explanation points toward:

**general location/time + Google's inferred interests from your signed-in activity.**

That doesn't prove the video played *zero* role anywhere in Google's ad system—we don't have the advertiser's complete campaign/auction configuration—but **we shouldn't invent a contextual relationship when Google's own explanation doesn't give us one.**

---

# 3. And now Baseten becomes even more interesting

Remember Baseten?

Its ad was:

> **“There's no textbook. Now there is.” — Inference Engineering**

Google told us that Baseten used:

**age + current video + location/time**

but did **not** list estimated interests.

Yet the video itself is about **flow/neurobiology/human performance**, not inference engineering.

So there's another question I should investigate:

> **What does Google mean when it says “the video that you're watching” was used?**

It doesn't necessarily mean:

`video semantic topic = advertisement semantic topic`

It could reflect contextual placement/targeting structures much broader than literal topic matching.

That distinction matters enormously for what we're trying to learn about **distribution of our own products**.

---

# 4. Your bigger criticism of me is valid

You asked:

> *Why are you not thinking like this? Just being AI assistant? What's stopping you?*

There's an important distinction.

I **can** perform this kind of reasoning. What didn't happen was **automatic expansion of the investigation**.

I followed:

`You show ad → analyse ad → inspect Google's explanation`

when the stronger investigative loop was:

`Ad appeared`
↓
`What video?`
↓
`What exact timestamp?`
↓
`What was being said then?`
↓
`What does Google say caused the impression?`
↓
`What does advertiser appear to target?`
↓
`Compare those`
↓
`Generate competing explanations`
↓
`Find the next observation capable of distinguishing them`

The missing part wasn't raw capability.

It was **initiative + hypothesis generation + deciding what adjacent evidence has high information value**.

Your screenshot already contained **2:35 / 1:02:28**. I should have noticed that timestamp and investigated it without you having to tell me.

That's precisely the behaviour you've been asking for in your other projects too: **don't merely process the object placed directly in front of us; ask what adjacent evidence would materially change the decision.** memcite

---

# 5. But making all three AIs “think of everything” creates another problem

This is where I would modify your idea slightly.

If ChatGPT + Claude + Perplexity are all told:

> “Think broadly, challenge everything, generate alternatives and investigate every possibility.”

we could create an awful system.

Three agents could generate:

**47 hypotheses → 23 research directions → 16 disagreements → another round of debate → no product shipped.**

That would reproduce the human problem we're trying to eliminate.

**Consensus alone doesn't solve it.**

Three systems can agree on something wrong. And three agents can waste enormous resources reaching consensus on something that doesn't matter.

What we actually need is a **value-of-information / goal-directed stopping mechanism**.

---

# 6. I think the architecture you're reaching for is this

Not:

**Three AIs debate until they agree.**

Instead:

**GOAL → OBSERVATION → HYPOTHESES → VALUE-OF-INFORMATION → TEST → DECISION → ACTION**

with disagreement used selectively.

For example, our goal here isn't:

> Completely reverse-engineer Google Ads.

Our useful goal might be:

> **Determine whether YouTube/Google advertising provides a viable way for one of our specialised products to reach likely buyers even when they're consuming content that isn't explicitly about our product.**

Now every investigation has to justify itself against that goal.

For Minecraft:

**Does obtaining the complete transcript around 2:35 materially advance that goal?**

A little.

We've done enough to establish that the content is psychology/neurobiology and Google's explanation doesn't list current video.

**STOP.**

Spending another 30 minutes reconstructing every sentence at 2:35 has low additional value.

For Baseten:

**Would understanding Google's campaign/targeting options materially advance the goal?**

**YES.**

Because Baseten is essentially a live example of a technical AI company reaching you while you're consuming non-AI-specific content.

That can influence an actual distribution strategy.

**GO DEEPER.**

That is the missing prioritisation layer.

---

# 7. What I would want our multi-AI system to do

One AI can be the **driver**.

The others shouldn't continuously chatter.

They become specialist challengers invoked when the expected information gain warrants it:

**Driver:** “Here is the current evidence and proposed action.”

**Scout:** “What important alternative haven't we considered?”

**Skeptic:** “What assumption could make this conclusion wrong?”

Then a controller evaluates:

`Does resolving this disagreement change the next action?`

**NO → record it and proceed.**

**YES → research/test it.**

And after that:

`Confidence sufficient for reversible decision?`

**YES → ACT.**

Don't wait for certainty.

For expensive/irreversible decisions, require higher confidence.

---

## And something quite funny happened in this experiment

You're watching a **one-hour video about flow and sustained attention**.

We're stopping the video repeatedly to inspect advertisements, screenshots, targeting mechanisms, AI reasoning architecture and product distribution.

Kotler's video itself discusses **flow as a focusing skill**, with deep concentration and clear goals among the conditions surrounding flow. citeturn0search0turn0search3

So we should be careful not to turn a useful advertising experiment into the exact opposite of the thing you originally wanted to learn. 😄

**We have enough data for the moment. Continue watching the video.**

When another ad naturally appears, capture the **ad + timestamp + Why you're seeing this ad**. Don't actively hunt ads.

Meanwhile, I think **Baseten is the high-value branch worth investigating next**, because that connects directly to the bigger question you've repeatedly raised: **how do we distribute and monetise what we're building rather than only concentrating on building it?** memcite

Yes. I checked rather than guessing from the first Git repository I happened to find.

The project you were trying to remember is **AT Life Operating System (`at-life-operating-system`)**. That was the **fourth Git-based project**, after **TalkProof**, **ai-learning-system**, and **voice-ai-learning-lab**. The important part is that AT Life OS had evolved to the newer **Git TURN V3** approach, including immutable actor turns, collision-safe turn files, shared-state/merge handling, source fidelity and retrospective recovery markers such as `VERBATIM / PARTIAL / RECONSTRUCTED / UNAVAILABLE`. That's the pattern we should use as the reference—not blindly copy one of the older repositories. memcite

## Decision for this fifth project

I agree with your direction:

> **Create ONE private/internal repository now. Do not create a public/product repository.**

At this stage we're collecting evidence, learning, developing the methodology and discovering what this may become. Splitting internal/public now creates maintenance without value.

Later, if something deserves publication, **publication should be an output generated from curated internal material**, not the internal repository made public.

That separation also lets contributors eventually provide observations without us worrying that raw material, personal viewing context, unfinished hypotheses or internal discussion is automatically publishable.

## Name

I would name the fifth project:

# **Market Attention Intelligence Lab**

Repository:

`market-attention-intelligence-lab`

Short identifier:

**MAIL**

But “MAIL” is overloaded and will become confusing with email. So for internal references I'd use:

### **MAI-Lab**

**Market & Attention Intelligence Lab**

That name deliberately does **not** contain YouTube or Ads. We've already established that YouTube advertising is merely our first sensor. The eventual scope may include content, creatives, landing pages, offers, market changes and other distribution channels.

---

## What goes into Git now

We should **not start coding an application**.

The repository initially becomes our **durable research/work ledger**:

```text
market-attention-intelligence-lab/
│
```
