Agreed. I'll make the design decision rather than adding more fields just because we can.

## Decision: keep the full provenance **inside the file**, not in every filename

The filename's job is **identification, sorting, collision avoidance and automation**. It should not try to become the database.

So the V004 standard should be:

```text
<PROJECT>_<PROCESSOR>_<TYPE>_<SEQ>_<DESCRIPTION>_<YYYYMMDD_HHMM>.<ext>
```

For example:

```text
MAILAB_CHATGPT_TURN_0001_PROJECT-FORMATION_20261010_2327.md

MAILAB_CHATGPT_OBSERVATION_0001_BASETEN_20261010_2327.md

MAILAB_PERPLEXITY_ANALYSIS_0003_AD-TARGETING-HYPOTHESES_20261015_1840.md
```

Why retain **processor/AI** in the filename? Because when multiple AIs work independently, seeing `CHATGPT`, `PERPLEXITY`, or `CLAUDE` immediately helps us distinguish parallel work and avoid collisions.

But I would **not** normally put `SENTHIL`, `MADANRAJ`, `SUBHA`, etc. in the filename.

That creates long names and unnecessarily exposes contributor identity when files are copied around.

---

## Full provenance lives at the top of the file

Every observation gets a standard header:

```yaml
project: Market & Attention Intelligence Lab
project_code: MAILAB

record_type: observation
record_id: OBS-000001
version: 001

observer: SENTHIL
submitter: SENTHIL
processor: CHATGPT
reviewers: []

observed_at: 2026-10-10T...
processed_at: 2026-10-10T...

source_platform: YouTube
source_fidelity: VERBATIM
evidence_status: RAW

publication_status: INTERNAL
```

Later:

```yaml
observer: MADANRAJ
submitter: SENTHIL
processor: CHATGPT
```

Nothing else needs changing.

And when contributors become numerous, these become IDs rather than names:

```yaml
observer_id: H0007
submitter_id: H0001
processor_id: AI-CHATGPT
```

Then a contributor registry resolves them.

We **don't need that complexity now**.

---

# One important change: don't encode everything in Markdown forever

You've identified something important when you call this **real-life data**.

Eventually there could be thousands of observations.

At that point Git Markdown files alone become a poor analytical database.

So our architecture should deliberately preserve three layers:

```text
        REAL WORLD
            │
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  1. RAW EVIDENCE       │
│ screenshots            │
│ transcripts            │
│ URLs / page snapshots  │
│ advertiser disclosures │
└───────────┬────────────┘
            │
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│ 2. STRUCTURED RECORDS  │
│ advertiser             │
│ payer                  │
│ creative               │
│ placement              │
│ targeting disclosure   │
│ source video           │
│ time                   │
│ observer               │
│ landing page           │
│ etc.                   │
└───────────┬────────────┘
            │
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│ 3. INTELLIGENCE        │
│ recurrence             │
│ patterns               │
│ hypotheses             │
│ market changes         │
│ experiments            │
│ product opportunities  │
└────────────────────────┘
```

Git initially holds all three in a transparent, inspectable form.

If volume becomes large, Layer 2 can migrate into **SQLite/Postgres/Parquet/etc.** without destroying Layer 1 provenance.

That is much safer than designing a database prematurely today.

---

# And you're right about the economic nature of the evidence

But I want to make one precision correction.

An ad impression is evidence that **a real advertising system selected and served an impression associated with an advertiser/campaign**.

It does **not automatically tell us**:

- what that advertiser bid;
- how much that particular impression cost;
- whether the advertiser was profitable;
- which targeting criterion dominated;
- how much campaign budget exists;
- whether seeing the same ad repeatedly means it is successful.

Those become hypotheses or require additional evidence.

That's exactly why this dataset can become valuable: we preserve **what actually happened** without quietly converting it into claims we haven't proved.

---

# Final V004 principle

I would add this prominently:

> ## **Evidence is immutable; interpretation is revisable.**

If today we record:

```text
OBSERVED:
Minecraft advertisement displayed while YouTube video remained visible.
```

that remains.

If ChatGPT says:

```text
INFERENCE:
Mid-roll advertisement.
```

and you later correct me, we don't rewrite history pretending the error never occurred.

We record:

```text
UNLEARN:
Mid-roll classification unsupported.

RELEARN:
Outside-player/watch-page sponsored placement.
```

That gives future AIs something far more valuable than a clean dataset:

**the history of how our understanding improved.**

---

## So V004 is now sufficiently defined for MAI-Lab bootstrap

I would stop designing the governance here. Further architecture right now has diminishing value.

Our agreed baseline is now:

**Private-first repository → README in every meaningful folder → standard standalone filenames → full provenance inside files → Observer/Submitter/Processor/Reviewer → raw/structured/intelligence separation → immutable evidence/revisable interpretation → daily WORKLOG → immutable TURNs → page-closure protocol → explicit public-promotion gate → future database only when volume justifies it.**

That's enough.

The next useful action is no longer another protocol discussion: **create the private `market-attention-intelligence-lab` repository.** Once you give me the repo, we bootstrap it from this V004 baseline and preserve everything we've already learned before continuing the experiment.

## Baseten: what Google actually says

For **Baseten Labs' “There's no textbook. Now there is.” / Inference Engineering** ad, Google's panel says the information used was:

- **Your age**
- **The video you're watching**
- **The time of day or your general location** — country/city

### That makes this experiment more interesting

Compare the two consecutive ads at the beginning of exactly the **same Big Think video**:

| | Specsavers | Baseten Labs |
|---|---|---|
| Same video | ✅ | ✅ |
| Same viewing session | ✅ | ✅ |
| ~same time | ✅ | ✅ |
| Age | Used | Used |
| Video being watched | Used | Used |
| Time/general location | Used | Used |
| Google's estimated interests/activity | **Used** | **Not listed** |
| Product | Eye examinations | AI inference-engineering book |
| Apparent connection to your AI work/interests | Weak | **Very strong** |

That last row is **our observation**, not Google's stated explanation.

And that's precisely the distinction we want to preserve.

## There's another discovery here

The Specsavers ad isn't merely a random optical-shop ad.

Your screenshot's small print says:

> **“Funded by the Scottish Government and available in Scotland only.”**

So its appearance makes considerable sense through the **general-location** signal Google disclosed.

Google explicitly says **the video you're watching was information used to show the Baseten ad**. That doesn't necessarily mean the advertiser literally targeted that exact video. Google's explanation doesn't expose the complete campaign configuration, bidding/audience logic, or tell us the weight assigned to each listed signal.

## Why this matters for our earlier product-distribution discussion

This is actual evidence of the thing we were trying to understand.

A company selling a **specialist technical AI/engineering resource** can reach somebody while they're watching content that isn't literally titled:

> “AI inference engineering”

So when we think about distributing one of our enterprise/AI products, the model shouldn't simply be:

**User searches our exact problem → our ad appears.**

There can potentially be:

**person/audience/context eligibility + video/content context + geography/time + advertiser targeting + auction/bid/quality → ad impression.**

And your two consecutive ads demonstrate that **different campaigns can reach the same person in the same content session through different disclosed combinations of signals.**

That's considerably more useful than the Wise example.

### Keep the experiment running

Don't alter My Ad Centre settings. You don't need to photograph everything anymore.

For each **new advertiser**, capture just:

1. **The ad itself**
2. **About this advertiser**
3. **The complete “Why you're seeing this ad” section**

That's enough.

And if **Baseten appears again on a completely different type of video**, that's particularly valuable. Then we'll have the beginnings of evidence for whether this is strongly content-dependent or follows you across unrelated content.

**Current sample: Wise → Specsavers → Baseten.** Let's keep accumulating observations rather than deciding the mechanism from only three advertisers.

You started the ~19-minute video, but around **6–7 minutes in**, you restarted it because while listening, **your attention had moved onto thoughts about work**. You wanted to hear that section/content properly again.

So approximately:

**First viewing:** ~6–7 min

→ **restart video from beginning**

You can have been **watching for ~30 minutes even though the actual video is ~19 minutes** because your elapsed real-world time includes ads, pauses, rewinds, switching apps, reading comments, etc. I wouldn't infer your viewing duration from the video's runtime.

Your screenshot is clearly a **YouTube sponsored ad from Wise** ("Stop paying for hidden fees", send money abroad).

But we **cannot conclude that YouTube showed Wise because of this specific video**. Google's own documentation says YouTube ad selection can combine several signals: videos you've watched, Google searches, apps/device activity, previous ad interactions, general geographic location, age range/account information, and interactions with YouTube. citeturn0search4turn0view0

There are two broad possibilities:

**1. Contextual targeting:** Google can choose an ad based on the current/recent video context, active searches, time, or general location—even when personalized advertising isn't being used. citeturn0view0

**2. Personalized/audience targeting:** if personalization is enabled, Google says your saved Google activity—including searches, YouTube videos watched, Android apps, ads/content interacted with, and general area—can contribute to ad selection. citeturn0view0

So the Wise ad could have been triggered by **you/audience characteristics rather than the content of `lgErkgdMrmk`**. That would also explain your important observation:

> **Other ads appeared during the same video and weren't related to the video.**

That's completely compatible with YouTube's advertising system. Advertisers can be competing for the same impression based on different eligibility/targeting criteria; the winning ad does not need to match the video's subject exactly.

### We can actually investigate *this* Wise impression

Don't rely on memory for the other ads. **Next time one appears, take exactly the kind of screenshot you just took before skipping it.**

For the Wise one, tap the **ⓘ next to "Sponsored"** (or the three-dot/ad controls if that's what YouTube presents). Google's **"Why this ad?" / My Ad Center** information can expose why Google says that particular ad was shown and provides access to the relevant ad controls. citeturn0search1turn0view0

That is much stronger evidence than us guessing from the video topic.
